Witch of Endor
wich uv EN-dor
noun phrase (a medium consulted by Saul)
From Endor, a town of Manasseh, and “witch” (Old English wicce); the woman with a familiar spirit whom Saul consulted on the eve of his death.

📖 Biblical Definition

The witch of Endor was the woman with a familiar spirit whom Saul, abandoned by God and terrified before the Philistine host, secretly consulted on the night before his death. Saul, who had earlier put the mediums and wizards out of the land in obedience to the law, now in his extremity disguised himself and sought one out, asking her to bring up Samuel. When Samuel appeared—to the woman's own terror—he pronounced Saul's doom: the kingdom rent away, and on the morrow Saul and his sons with him among the dead. The Chronicler gives the LORD's own verdict on the king's end: “Saul died… for asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit, to enquire of it; and enquired not of the LORD.” The dictionary marks the witch of Endor as Scripture's solemn condemnation of all necromancy, spiritism, and consulting of the dead, which the law of God expressly forbids—the charmer, the consulter with familiar spirits, the wizard, the necromancer are an abomination to the LORD. Whether Samuel truly appeared by God's sovereign act (the most natural reading of the text) or by some other means, the lesson is fixed: Saul's recourse to the dead in place of the living God was the final seal of his apostasy and the immediate cause named for his death. The dictionary holds the account against both the modern dismissal of the demonic as superstition and the occult fascination that would dabble in mediums and séances; the living are to seek the living God, and the law's sentence on spiritism stands unrepealed.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The medium of Endor whom the doomed Saul consulted to bring up Samuel on the eve of his death (1 Samuel 28); Scripture's condemnation of necromancy and spiritism, and the named cause of Saul's death (1 Chronicles 10:13).

expand to see more

WITCH OF ENDOR, noun phrase. The woman with a familiar spirit consulted by Saul before his death.

Saul, abandoned by God, sought her to bring up Samuel (1 Samuel 28:7-11).

Samuel pronounced Saul's doom: defeat and death on the morrow.

The law forbids the consulter with familiar spirits and the necromancer (Deuteronomy 18:11).

Saul died for enquiring of a familiar spirit and not of the LORD (1 Chronicles 10:13).

📖 Key Scripture

1 Sa 28:7 — "Then said Saul unto his servants, Seek me a woman that hath a familiar spirit, that I may go to her, and enquire of her. And his servants said to him, Behold, there is a woman that hath a familiar spirit at Endor."

1 Sa 28:11 — "Then said the woman, Whom shall I bring up unto thee? And he said, Bring me up Samuel."

De 18:11 — "Or a charmer, or a consulter with familiar spirits, or a wizard, or a necromancer."

1 Ch 10:13 — "So Saul died for his transgression which he committed against the LORD, even against the word of the LORD, which he kept not, and also for asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit, to enquire of it;"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The modern dismissal treats the demonic and the occult as mere superstition; the opposite error indulges an occult fascination with mediums and séances. Both defy the law that forbids consulting the dead.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the law's standing prohibition of spiritism and the living God as the only One to be consulted. One error, the rationalist, dismisses the whole account as primitive superstition—no real spirit, no real judgment—and so denies both the reality of the demonic and the seriousness of Saul's sin. The dictionary answers from the text and from the law: the consulting of familiar spirits is named an abomination, and the Chronicler records that Saul died for it. The unseen world is real, and traffic with it against God's command is deadly.

The opposite and equally forbidden error is the occult fascination of the age—mediums, séances, channelling, the consulting of the dead dressed up as entertainment or comfort. Saul's example is the warning: a man may put away such things outwardly and yet return to them in his extremity when he has forsaken the LORD. The dictionary holds the law's sentence unrepealed: the living are to seek the living God through His Word, not the dead through forbidden arts. Whatever the precise manner of Samuel's appearing, the lesson is fixed—to seek counsel of the dead in place of God is the seal of apostasy and the road to ruin.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Endor (Hebrew 'Ein-Dor, “spring of Dor”), a town of Manasseh, and the “familiar spirit” (Hebrew 'ob) the woman possessed; “witch” from the Old English wicce.

expand to see more

'Ein-Dor, Hebrew, “spring of Dor,” a town of Manasseh.

'Ob, Hebrew, a “familiar spirit” or the medium possessed by it.

Wicce, Old English, a witch or sorceress.

The necromancer (Hebrew doresh el-ha-metim, “one who seeks the dead”), forbidden in Deuteronomy 18:11.

Saul had earlier “put away those that had familiar spirits… out of the land” (1 Samuel 28:3).

Usage

"The pastor preached the witch of Endor to condemn all consulting of the dead, which the law forbids."

"He warned against the occult fascination of the age, naming Saul's recourse to the medium his final apostasy."

"She saw that Saul died for seeking a familiar spirit and enquiring not of the LORD."
